deep.reconstruction:
Notation: Riemann's (x) is the sawtooth of his Habilitation, x minus the nearest integer, with (x)=0 at half-integers. E(y) is the integer part, so (y)=y-E(y+1/2). p runs over odd numbers, and (-1)^{(p-1)/2}=chi_4(p).

A. A character-weighted Riemann series at rational points. Riemann considers F(x)=Sum_{p odd} (-1)^{(p-1)/2}(px)/p, a chi_4-twisted analogue of his Habilitation series Sum (nx)/n^k. He evaluates it at x=m/n, where (px) depends only on p mod n.
- n odd: write p=p'+2ns. Then (-1)^{(p-1)/2}=(-1)^{(p'-1)/2}(-1)^{ns}=(-1)^{(p'-1)/2}(-1)^s. So F(m/n)=Sum_{p'} (-1)^{(p'-1)/2}(p'm/n) Sum_s (-1)^s/(2ns+p'). The inner sums converge (alternating), so F is finite there.
- n even: the factor (-1)^{ns} is 1. The inner sums Sum_s 1/(2ns+p') diverge, so convergence needs the finite sum Sum_{p' odd mod 2n} (-1)^{(p'-1)/2}(p'm/n) to vanish.
- He reduces to Sum_{p=1}^{n-1} chi(p)(pm/n)=Sum chi(p)(pm/n - E(pm/n+1/2)) and notes 'n = 2 mod 4'.
- (My completion.) For n=2 mod 4 we have chi(n-p)=chi(p) and ((n-p)m/n)=-(pm/n), so the half-sum vanishes. Also chi(n+p)=-chi(p) with equal sawtooth values, so the full period sum vanishes too.
- (My completion.) For 4|n the terms pair up equally instead of cancelling. So F(m/n) generally diverges logarithmically when 4 divides the denominator.
- The fragment 'n-1-n/2' is the start of an unfinished count of the E-terms.

B. Fourier series of the sawtooth. From log(1+x)=Sum(-1)^{n-1}x^n/n with x=e^{i phi}:
- 2 log(1+e^{i phi}) = log(4cos^2(phi/2)) + 2pi i (phi/2pi) = 2 Sum (-1)^{n-1}cos(n phi)/n + 2i Sum (-1)^{n-1} sin(n phi)/n.
- The argument of 1+e^{i phi} is phi/2 for |phi|<pi. Writing it with the sawtooth makes the formula valid for all phi.
- Imaginary part with phi=2pi x: (x)=(1/pi) Sum_{n>=1} (-1)^{n-1} sin(2pi n x)/n.

C. Series in sawtooth functions (Dirichlet convolution). Put phi'(x)=Sum_s a_s sin(2pi s x). Then:
- Sum_s a_s(sx) = (1/pi) Sum_n ((-1)^{n-1}/n) phi'(nx).
- Collecting terms with N=theta*theta': Sum_s a_s(sx) = (1/pi) Sum_N sin(2pi N x) Sum_{theta*theta'=N} (-1)^{theta'-1} a_theta/theta'.
- So the Fourier coefficients of Sum a_s(sx) are the Dirichlet convolution of a with ((-1)^{n-1}/n). This can be inverted to expand a given sine series in sawtooth functions (cf. Davenport 1937).
- (My remark.) For a_s=chi_4(s)/s and N odd, the coefficient is (1/(pi N)) Sum_{d|N} chi_4(d) = r_2(N)/(4 pi N). This links part A to sums of two squares.

D. Lambert/Euler-product inversion.
- -Sum_n a_n log(1-q^n) = Sum_n Sum_s a_n q^{ns}/s = Sum_s f(q^s)/s, where f(q)=Sum a_n q^n.
- This is the generating-function form of the Moebius inversion on the previous page. There, Gauss's count of irreducible polynomials, [z^{pq}-z^p-z^q+z]/pq, corresponds to f(q)=zq.
- (My interpretation.) On |q|=1 with q=e^{2pi i x}, Im(-log(1-q^n)) is a sawtooth in nx. So sums Sum a_n(nx) are boundary values of this function, which links C and D.
- He then chooses f(q) = 1 - (log((1+q)/(1-q))/(2q))^{-alpha} = 1-(artanh(q)/q)^{-alpha}. Note f(0)=0. The other jottings are '1-(q/pi)^alpha' and a unit circle marked +-1, +-i.

E. Behaviour of artanh(q)/q on the unit circle.
- For q=e^{-i phi}, 0<phi<2pi: log((1+q)/(1-q)) = (1/2)log(cot^2(phi/2)) +- (pi/2) i.
- With alpha=cot^2(phi/2), q=(sqrt(alpha) -+ i)/(sqrt(alpha) +- i) and 1/(2q)=(alpha-1 +- 2 sqrt(alpha) i)/(2(alpha+1)).
- The product is (alpha-1 -+ 2 sqrt(alpha) i)/(2(alpha+1)) * ((1/2)log alpha +- (pi/2) i), with the upper/lower sign conventions as written.
- Real part: (1/4) log(alpha)(alpha-1)/(alpha+1) + pi sqrt(alpha)/(2(alpha+1)).
- Imaginary part: +-[(pi/4)(alpha-1)/(alpha+1) - sqrt(alpha) log(alpha)/(2(alpha+1))].
- Replacing sqrt(alpha) by alpha, Im = [(pi/4)(alpha-1/alpha) - log alpha]/(alpha+1/alpha).
- The numerator has derivative (pi/4)(1+1/alpha^2) - 1/alpha. Its zeros are alpha = 2/pi +- sqrt(4/pi^2-1), which are not real since pi>2. So the numerator is strictly increasing, with its only zero at alpha=1 (q=+-i, where artanh(q)/q = pi/4).
- Derivative of the quotient (numerator of the quotient rule): (pi/4)(1+1/alpha^2)-1/alpha)(alpha+1/alpha) - (1-1/alpha^2)((pi/4)(alpha-1/alpha) - log alpha). This simplifies to pi/alpha - (1+1/alpha^2) + (1-1/alpha^2) log alpha.
- Dividing by (1-1/alpha^2) gives the extremum condition (pi-(alpha+1/alpha))/(alpha-1/alpha) + log alpha = 0.
- Its derivative times (alpha-1/alpha)^2 is (1/alpha)(alpha-1/alpha)^2 - (1-1/alpha^2)(alpha-1/alpha) - (pi-(alpha+1/alpha))(1+1/alpha^2).
- Purpose (my inference): to control the argument and extrema of artanh(q)/q on |q|=1, so that the power (.)^{-alpha} in f is single-valued and its boundary behaviour (and hence the size of a_n) can be judged. The exponent alpha of f and the parameter alpha=cot^2(phi/2) are different quantities that Riemann denotes by the same letter.
errors: The line 'log(1+e^{phi i}) = Sum...' has a factor 2 on both sides in the manuscript, consistent with the next line. Not an error, but the machine transcription drops it.

The ninth line from the bottom contains a slip that is corrected immediately below it: the derivative factor is written (pi/4)(1+1/alpha^2) - 4/(alpha pi), and probably intended as (pi/4)(1+1/alpha^2) - 1/alpha. The quadratic root alpha = 2/pi +- sqrt(4/pi^2-1) and the quotient-rule line use -1/alpha.
In the last long line the factor is written (pi - alpha + 1/alpha) instead of (pi - (alpha+1/alpha)). Riemann corrects this in the line beneath.
The finite-sum reduction for even n (Sum_{1,pn-1}, probably Sum_{1,2n-1}) is left incomplete and partly crossed out. The convergence criterion for 4|n is not stated explicitly.
Interchanging the order of summation in C is formal; for discontinuous (x) it needs the usual justification (convergence in the mean or at points of continuity). This is not addressed.

results.what: Evaluation of Sum_p chi_4(p)(px)/p at x=m/n. It reduces to finite character sums times Sum_s (-1)^s/(2ns+p) for odd n; for even n the reduction is to a cancellation condition that holds for n=2 mod 4.
results.modern_name: Twisted Riemann/Hecke-type sawtooth series at rational points; Dedekind-sum-like finite character sums
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Habilitation 1854) for the untwisted Sum (nx)/n^k; twisted versions studied by Hardy-Littlewood, Davenport, Chowla (20th c.)

results.what: (x) = (1/pi) Sum (-1)^{n-1} sin(2 pi n x)/n, derived from log(1+e^{i phi})
results.modern_name: Fourier series of the sawtooth function
results.usually_credited_to: Euler/Fourier/Dirichlet; used by Riemann in Habilitation

results.what: Sum a_s(sx) = (1/pi) Sum_N sin(2 pi N x) Sum_{theta*theta'=N} (-1)^{theta'-1} a_theta/theta'. Fourier coefficients of a sawtooth series are a Dirichlet convolution, which can be inverted.
results.modern_name: Expansion of functions in series of sawtooth functions (Davenport-type identities, Hecke operators on periodic functions)

deep.surprise_reason: Most of the page is routine: the sawtooth Fourier series, the Lambert-series identity and elementary calculus on the unit circle. Two points are mildly notable. First, Riemann treats general series Sum a_s(sx) and writes their Fourier coefficients as a Dirichlet convolution, with an implicit inversion. Second, he studies a chi_4-twisted sawtooth series at rationals, finding a convergence dichotomy by denominator mod 4. This anticipates Davenport-style sawtooth-series identities of the 1930s, but only formally and without conclusions, consistent with his Habilitation work on Sum (nx)/n^k.

transcription_corrections: f q = -( log((1+q)/(1-q)) / (2q) )^{-alpha} + 1. A minus sign precedes the bracket, so f(0)=0.
The line on log(1+e^{phi i}) reads '2 log(1+e^{phi i}) = 2 Sum (-1)^{n-1} e^{n phi i}/n'.
'Sum_{1,pn-1}' is probably 'Sum_{1,2n-1}' (sum over a full period of odd residues mod 2n).
phi'_x = Sum a_s sin(s x 2pi) defines the sine series; the leading 'n=' before it is cancelled in the manuscript.
In the line after the Im formula, the second expression reads (pi/4)(1+1/alpha^2) - (something)/(alpha pi); as used afterwards it should be -1/alpha.
The last long line has (pi - alpha + 1/alpha), corrected beneath to (pi - (alpha+1/alpha)).
